paras: The lynching of William Moore was the killing of a Black man by a mob in southern Mississippi on May 20, 1919, after he was accused of shooting the manager of a sawmill or lumber camp. Black newspapers placed the lynching at McHenry or near Ten Mile and reported that Moore was taken from a train and hanged from a tree. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) cited the case in a telegram to Governor Theodore G. Bilbo, counting it as the fifth lynching in Mississippi in less than three months.

Moore was described in a wire report as "a Negro of Gulfport, Miss.," and in later Black-press accounts as an alleged bootlegger. According to the wire report, datelined McHenry on May 21, he was alleged to have shot and killed J. H. Rogers, the manager of a saw mill. The Baltimore Afro-American and the NAACP said instead that he had shot the manager of a lumber camp while being arrested, without stating whether the manager died.

After the shooting, a posse was organized when word came that Moore was aboard a southbound Gulf and Ship Island Railroad train, according to a Ten Mile dispatch in the Afro-American. Members of the posse boarded the train at Ten Mile, removed him, and hanged him from a nearby tree. The NAACP's account, which gave the date as May 20, said he was taken from the train by a mob, hanged to a tree, and his body "riddled with bullets."

The McHenry wire report was briefer, saying only that Moore "was caught by a mob and lynched" shortly after the shooting. None of the accounts gives the size of the group, names any of its members, or mentions officers at the scene.

On May 24 the NAACP's secretary, John R. Shillady, telegraphed Bilbo on behalf of 210 branches and 54,000 members in 39 states to ask what Mississippi authorities were doing to apprehend Moore's lynchers. The telegram also listed the burning of Lloyd Clay at Vicksburg, a reported double lynching near Pickens, and an earlier case, saying state authorities had done nothing in any of them. It warned that Mississippi's failure to enforce its own laws justified the migration of Black residents to places where they would be protected and made federal intervention inevitable.
No report of an inquest, an arrest, or a reply from the governor appears in the coverage.

News of the lynching first reached Black readers through a short wire item, which the St. Louis Argus printed on its front page on May 23 under the headline "Another Mississippi Lynching." The Argus set it among other lynching reports, including a Georgia case and an Associated Negro Press dispatch on public alarm at "the recent epidemic of lynchings in various sections of the South." The Colorado Statesman ran a one-sentence version among general news briefs the next day.

The Baltimore Afro-American's May 30 dispatch was more pointed, opening with the remark that Mississippi had beaten "its own record" and calling Moore the fifth man killed by a mob in the state in under 100 days. The NAACP release appeared in the Dayton Forum on June 6 under the headline "Mississippi Governor Again Asked If Lynchers Are To Be Prosecuted," and in the Dallas Express the following day. In these later versions the case was presented as part of an argument that Mississippi was failing to prosecute lynchers.

The accounts differ on place and on the alleged crime: the wire report placed the lynching at McHenry and said Rogers was killed, while the Afro-American and the NAACP placed it at or near Ten Mile and said only that Moore shot a lumber camp manager. In the Argus, the McHenry item was preceded by a paragraph describing a great crowd of onlookers, a body "roasting over the fire," and two white men shot during "the struggles attending the lynching." No other account of Moore's death mentions fire or a crowd, and the NAACP's telegram reported that Lloyd Clay had been burned to death at Vicksburg ten days earlier, which suggests the paragraph belongs to that case rather than to Moore's.

reader.title: Lynching of William Moore
bases: Every account says Moore was seized by a mob or posse after an alleged shooting and lynched, the fuller versions saying he was taken from a train and hanged (A2, A4, A7).

Moore was hanged by a 'mob' (A2, A7) or by 'members of the posse' (A4) who took him from a train, with no legal process, in retaliation for his alleged shooting of a mill or lumber camp manager (A2, A4, A7).

The McHenry wire item (A2, A3), the Ten Mile dispatch (A4) and the NAACP release (A7) agree that Moore was lynched by a mob on or about May 20 after an alleged shooting of a manager, though they differ on place and details.
